blocks.content: A taint is applied to a node, and by default, it repels every Pod from being scheduled there, unless that Pod explicitly tolerates it, covered in the next topic.
1. Applied to a Node, Repelling Pods
blocks.text: 1. Applied to a Node, Repelling Pods

blocks.content: Unlike affinity rules, which live on a Pod and describe where it wants to go, a taint lives on a node and describes what it refuses to accept, by default, an ordinary Pod simply will not be scheduled onto a tainted node at all.

blocks.alt: A node actively repelling Pods, by default, until told otherwise

blocks.content: A taint has one of three effects: NoSchedule (new Pods without a matching toleration are simply not placed here), PreferNoSchedule (a soft version, avoided if possible, but not strictly forbidden), and NoExecute (the strictest, covered below).

blocks.alt: Three distinct levels of severity, from a soft preference to a strict rule

blocks.content: 3. This Is How Control Plane Nodes Stay Clear
blocks.text: 3. This Is How Control Plane Nodes Stay Clear

blocks.content: This directly explains a fact stated back in the Architecture module's Control Plane topic, control plane nodes typically carry a taint by default, keeping ordinary application Pods off of them entirely, unless something explicitly tolerates it.

blocks.alt: The exact mechanism behind control plane nodes staying free of application Pods

blocks.content: NoExecute is the strictest effect, it does not just prevent new Pods from scheduling there, it actively evicts any Pods already running on that node that do not tolerate it, this is genuinely used when a node is being drained or marked unhealthy.

blocks.alt: Actively removing existing Pods, not just blocking new ones

blocks.content: 5. The Node's Side of a Two-Part System
blocks.text: 5. The Node's Side of a Two-Part System

blocks.content: A taint alone only tells half the story, it is deliberately paired with tolerations, covered in the very next topic, applied to Pods, together they form a complete, two-sided mechanism.

blocks.alt: One half of a deliberate two-part system, the Pod's side is covered next

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A taint is applied to a node and repels Pods by default, with three effects ranging from a soft preference (PreferNoSchedule) to active eviction (NoExecute).
This is exactly how control plane nodes stay clear of application workloads by default, and it is designed as one half of a system completed by tolerations, covered next.
